utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon everyone in and around the courtroom. This is IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Today is Monday, the 16th of June, 2008. My greetings to the accused, the Defence counsel, the OTP representatives as well as all the people helping us out. First all I'm going to read out an oral decision. It may be long but I shall try to be swift. Oral decision on the filing by the Praljak Defence of the expert report of Slobodan Jankovic. On the 9th May, 2008, the Praljak Defence requested the Trial Chamber leave to file two expert reports by Slobodan Jankovic titled: Analysis of HVO artillery, HVO in the Mostar sector. Analysis of the destruction of the old bridge on the basis of video recordings that are available further to Rule 94 bis. On the 27th of May, 2008, the Praljak Defence withdrew the report entitled analysis of HVO artillery, Croatian Defence Council in their Mostar Defence in its response of the 5th of June 2008, the Prosecution opposed the filing of the report entitled analysis of the old bridge on the basis of available video recordings and challenged the quality as an expert of Mr. Slobodan Jankovic as well as th relevance of his conclusions, his findings. According to the Prosecution, their witness based his opinion only on visual observation of the video recording of the destruction of the old Mostar bridge. Furthermore, the Prosecution requested leave to cross-examine the expert in question. The Trial Chamber deliberated on this issue and first notices -- first notes, sorry that Mr. Slobodan Jankovic has already testified as a Defence expert in the matter of ballistics in two prior cases in this Tribunal. Furthermore, upon reading the expert report and the author's CV, the Trial Chamber is of the view that Mr. Slobodan Jankovic is, on first impression, fit to testify, is qualified to testify as an expert in the matters he deals with in his report including in the analysis of video recordings showing the destruction of the old Mostar bridge. However, further to the Prosecution's application, the Trial Chamber is of the view that Mr. Slobodan Jankovic will have to appear before the Tribunal including for cross-examination purposes. The Prosecution will then have the opportunity to challenge his quality and qualifications as well as the validity and the relevance of his findings as expressed in the expert report. The Trial Chamber recalls that it is in light of the testimony of Mr. Slobodan Jankovic after he has testified that the Trial Chamber will rule on the report. According to the latest schedule, the witness should testify from the 30th of June to the 3rd of July, 2008, as a Defence expert for only the Praljak Defence. Mr. Praljak's Defence will examine the witness for an hour. The Trial Chamber decides that the cross-examination by the Prosecution will last one hour and a half. For the other Defence teams, it will be 30 minutes. So, in a nutshell, the Praljak Defence will have one hour, and the other Defence counsel for the other accused will have 30 minutes, the Prosecutor will have an hour and 30 minutes. The Trial Chamber will rule after all this as to the admissibility of the expert report. Very well, Mr. Karnavas, is your witness ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, he is, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Mr. President, good afternoon, Your Honours, yes, he is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll have him brought in, but I'll give Mr. Registrar the floor for a few IC numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Some parties have submitted lists of documents to be tendered through Witness 1D-AA. The list submitted by 1D shall be given Exhibit number IC 00804. The list of submitted by the OTP shall be given Exhibit number IC 00805. And the list submitted by 3D shall be given Exhibit number IC 00806. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Karnavas, we have five binders. When you want to use a document, please also name the number for the binder in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I'll try, Mr. President. And everybody should have a list as well in the order in which, as you will note, that it was passed around rather late, that was when we finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Good afternoon, sir. Let me first check that you can hear me in your language. If it is so, please tell me that you understand and hear me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please state your first name, surname and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mile Akmadzic, the 1st of October, 1939.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you had an opportunity to testify before a court as to the events that took place in the former Yugoslavia or is this the first time you are going to testify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the second time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you tell me when was the first time, in which case it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 2000, it was the Kordic trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were you a Defence or a Prosecution witness then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I forgot to ask you one thing. What is your current occupation or are you retired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am retired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please read out the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly swear that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. Please be seated. Some information, it won't be long because you have been a witness already so you know how the proceedings are going to unfold. First of all you will be asked questions by Mr. Prlic's counsel, Mr. Karnavas. You must have met with him as part of the preparation for this testimony. Mr. Karnavas is going to ask questions of you and submit documents to you. Once this is over, the OTP representative sitting on your right-hand side is going to ask questions of you as part of the cross-examination. The Prosecution will have the same amount of time as the Defence for their questions. You have four Judges in front of you. They, too, can ask questions. For purposes of efficiency, we usually ask questions once the Defence and the Prosecutor have finished asking their questions but it may be that when there is a special document that is worthy of further questions in order not to go back to the documents later on, the Judges may ask questions of you when the document is first shown to you. Try to be brief in your answers. If you fail to understand the meaning of a question, do not hesitate, ask for some clarification from the person asking you. If at any time during the hearing, you want to have a break, for instance because you're not feeling well or so, don't hesitate. We shall then have a break. We have breaks every 90 minutes, usually for 20 minutes. Sometimes exceptionally so, 15 minutes. So this is what I wanted to convey to you. Of course we are available to you if you have any questions. You have just made a solemn declaration, therefore from now on, you are a witness of the Court of justice even if you are called by Mr. Prlic's Defence. As such, from now on, you're not to have any contact with Mr. Prlic's counsel since now that you have made the solemn declaration, you are a witness of justice. This is also what I wanted to tell you. Mr. Karnavas, you have the floor unless there is -- yes, Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, one very brief matter. I do see at page 5, line 10 of the transcript and perhaps so the witness is not taken by surprise, of course after my learned friend, Mr. Karnavas has examined the witness in chief, he will be cross-examined by the Defence prior to the Prosecution. I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, you are absolutely right. I had forgotten about it. Once Mr. Karnavas has examined in chief, the other lawyers representing the other five accused can also ask questions of you as part of the cross-examination. Thank you, Mr. Khan, for filling the gap there for me. Mr. Karnavas, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Again, good afternoon, Mr. President, and Your Honour, Your Honours and everyone in and around the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Akmadzic.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. First I'm going to go through your background rather quickly. Unless there is any objections I'm going to be leading the witness to his background. As I understand it, you told us already that you were born in 1939, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And after graduating high school in 1965, I believe you graduated from the Sarajevo university in English, German and Latin languages; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: From approximately 1964 to 1978 you were working for, I believe, it was a large company Energoinvest as a translator primarily responsible for international matters?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: As a translator, yes, in international matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then in 1978, as I understand it, you began working for the Presidency of the then Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And as I understand it, you were an advisor on international protocol; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In 1982, you joined the organising committee for the 14th winter Olympic games that were held in Sarajevo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I take it you worked there up until the games and I believe the games were in 1984 so that would have been for a couple of years; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: That's right, until somewhere in mid-1984.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then in 1984, I believe you returned back to the Presidency where you were -- you headed the international protocol sector until about the beginning of 1990?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Then around February 1991 as I understand it, you were elected to the office of the general secretary of the Presidency of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: Let me try to be a little more specific. It was in mid-1990 that I was working with the office of the president of the Presidency and then in February 1991, I was appointed secretary general of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And you held that position, as I understand it, up until the time when you were elected prime minister of what became the republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that would have been around November 10, 1992; correct, when you were elected prime minister?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you held that position until about the end of -- sometime towards the middle or end of August 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: That's right, almost until the very end of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And we're going to go into some of that in greater detail, but -- and let me just go back a little bit. As I understand it, in -- in November 14th, 1992, you were elected one of the vice-presidents of the HDZ-BiH, that would have been -- correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So in other words, while you were holding that position within the Presidency, you also had a particular position within the HDZ which was a political party?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. The microphones pick up very well so you don't need to shout, you know. And I understand you might be nervous so a little water may help you calm down a little bit. Then, as I understand it, at some point in -- I believe it was December 10, 1993, you became a member of the presidential consul of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Then in early, I believe 1995, you were elected vice-president of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, the government of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That would have been before, before the Dayton Peace Accords?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well let's go back a little bit now that I've covered in rather general ways your background. At first I want to go into your position of being secretary -- general secretary of the Presidency. For those of us who are not aware of that position, could you please explain a little bit what this position entailed?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: The Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina comprised seven members and the secretary general who was appointed by the Presidency directly. This is a high-ranking administrative position and it is in charge of the general functioning of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina within the Presidency and outside the Presidency, as far as administrative aspects of its work were concerned, this is a position that carries some responsibility but is not of a political nature such as the positions occupied by the members of the Presidency and this position does not call for an appointment -- does not call for an election.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, I'm going to ask you to slow down a little bit because everything is being translated and at this pace, I'm afraid that they may not be able to keep up by the end of the afternoon so if you could show down just a little bit, okay? Now -- okay, good. Now, in your position as the general secretary, did you have the authority or the power to vote along with the presidents of the Presidency -- or the members of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: I didn't have the power to vote, but I had the power to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And as I understand it, and correct me if I am wrong, with respect to -- the minutes of the meetings were being taken; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And was your position such that you would have been responsible in part for those minutes or was somebody else responsible for it?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: Minutes were taken by someone else. I would go through them and at the next meeting of the Presidency, I would grant my approval.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now you say you would grant your approval and how would that approval be granted?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: I would just go through them and when I realised that I could go to a Presidency meeting then under the regulations at the next meeting of the Presidency would approve and adopt the minutes or perhaps amend them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, did the -- did the minutes themselves, once they were approved, did they require to be signed by anyone in order to demonstrate that they had been indeed looked at, reviewed, and approved?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: The minutes were signed by the president and the secretary general.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So that would have been you when you held that position?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, with respect to this Presidency, we heard a little bit about it but again, since you were one of the, for lack a better term, one of the insiders, could you please explain to us how did this Presidency function? What were the responsibilities of this Presidency and its members?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: As I said before, the Presidency comprised seven members elected directly by the people. Once the Presidency had been established after its first meeting, the president would be appointed. The president is equal to the other members of the Presidency except for one thing, he chairs the meetings and schedules the meetings of the Presidency and he also signs any decisions taken by the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And we've heard this term before but I want to see whether you can verify it. Is this known or -- yeah, is this known as a collective body?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, the Presidency is a collective head of state primarily of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina when it was still part Yugoslavia and then also of the sovereign Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: The Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I know there was a president of the Presidency, was there a position such as the vice-president of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: There was no such thing as the vice-president of the Presidency but when the president was abroad, somebody would always be appointed to stand in for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. With respect to the military, was it the president who was the commander in chief or was it this collective body?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: The collective body, the Presidency as a whole, was the supreme commander of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's leave the Presidency for a second and go to the government itself because we know that you served as prime minister. If you could tell always little bit, just very briefly, about the relationships between, say, the Presidency and the government itself? And when we speak of government, perhaps I should ask you first to explain what is meant by government by your system or the system back then?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: The government was one of the state bodies, one of the three state bodies. There was the Presidency, the head state firstly; secondly, the assembly as the legislative body and then the government as the executive body. I'm talking about Bosnia and Herzegovina. The legislative body of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that comprised presidents, the vice-presidents and it also had a secretary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now going back to my earlier question as far as the relation between the Presidency and the government, how did they interact with one subordinate to the other, could you help us out here a little bit?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: Under the constitution and the laws of Bosnia and Herzegovina, each of those bodies had their own powers and areas which they were in charge. Both of these bodies were bodies of the executive, the Presidency was the head of state and the government ran -- governed states in as far as any elements were concerned in relation to which it was bound to so under the law that applied.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: As I understand it, the government now had different various ministries one of which was the Ministry of Foreign Affairs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: As I understand it, prior to you becoming prime minister and even thereafter, the Minister for Foreign Affairs was Haris Silajdzic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if you could briefly explain to us the relationship between the ministry and, say, the prime minister and the president -- president of the Presidency. To whom would the minister be responsible and accountable to?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: The minister was responsible to the government and the prime minister and the president of the Presidency is one of the members of this collective body, the head of state. When invited by the Presidency, his minister can also submit a report however answering any other questions but as a matter of principle it goes through the prime minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, while you were there, not speaking prior to your being the prime minister, could you please explain to the Trial Chamber how often Mr. Silajdzic reported to you on his activity and we're going to talk a little bit approximate it but if you could just tell us briefly about that relationship?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Silajdzic, as foreign minister, spends a lot of time abroad. He did not submit any reports to the prime minister or indeed the government or indeed the Presidency. He only spoke to me once. He wanted to talk about his time abroad, and I warned him on that occasion that in the future, he should not travel abroad without obtaining approval previously from the government or indeed without so to speak a platform in terms of what he would be discussing there. On his return to the country, he should inform me first and then we would see together whether this was something for the government or the Presidency to deal with. However, he failed to follow suit. He did not comply with this decision of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well just to make sure that I understand it, because I'm familiar with my system back in the States with the Secretary of State, that's what we call the minister of foreign affairs, normally that position is not a policy position; in other words, the minister would not be designing and executing a particular policy of his or her own but rather it would be the government's or the executive, whatever is the executive authority would be setting the foreign policy with the minister merely executing it or implementing it. In that system of yours, could you please explain to us what was the authority of the foreign minister to be going around having trips, never reporting and God knows doing what during those trips while he was outside the country?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: Foreign minister of Bosnia and Herzegovina from the time it became an independent state, well, that is the time when actually Bosnia and Herzegovina had started to have foreign minister. Before that, this post was called something else. He is on an equal footing with other members of the government. He is not elected, an elected official, he is appointed at the recommendation of the president by the assembly. And since during the war the assembly could not be in session and he had already been appointed, he was confirmed, he was reappointed by the Presidency at my recommendation and the recommendation of the prime minister. When the foreign minister is abroad in accordance with the law on foreign affairs and in accordance with the discussions held with the prime minister, the president and the platform of the government, he is duty-bound to represent Bosnia and Herzegovina wherever it is that he actually has to represent it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, let me just sort of fast-forward all the way to the end of our discussion and then we'll go back and sort of fill in the pieces. From your CV, you were, from February 1991 until the -- until August 1993, a member of -- working with the Presidency and thereafter the prime minister and you would have been a member of the War Presidency at the time. Can you please tell us, summarize for us, during that period and even thereafter to your knowledge how was the Presidency functioning as an institution considering that it did have -- you did have a constitution and you had rules and regulations on how it was supposed to function and the responsibilities and authorities each member including the president of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: The Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina was established on the 20th of December, 1990 that's when it was constituted. That's when the president of the Presidency was elected, that was done at the first session and the term of office was one year. That's when the rules procedure of the first Presidency were also adopted and in accordance with the rules of procedure, the term of office of the president of the Presidency was one year; but after the expiry of this one year term of office, it could be extended by another year, but that was the maximum extension. The -- there was another criterion that was applied in Bosnia and Herzegovina and that was the following: The post of the president of the Presidency, the president of the assembly and the prime minister of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina were subject to rotation. In other words, officials from the three constituent peoples were to be appointed to those posts according to a system of rotation. The Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina from the 20th of December, 1990, until the 20th of December, 1991, functioned fully within the legislative framework in place in accordance with the constitution and in accordance with the rules of procedure of the Presidency. At the first session, the presidents of -- or chairman of various bodies of the Presidency were also appointed in addition to the president of the Presidency. One of those bodies was in charge of defence issues. It was headed ex officio by the president of the Presidency and the name of this body was the defence council. There was another body for the protection of the constitutional order and a member of the Presidency was in charge of that body. The third key body was the commission, the personnel commission in charge of appointments within Bosnia and Herzegovina to various posts, in particular, within the Presidency itself. So these were the three key bodies. There were two other bodies that were also within the purview of the Presidency such as the body that was -- that dealt with decorations and awards and another one that dealt with complaints, pardons, and there were perhaps some other working bodies that I cannot remember now. Each of those working bodies was headed by a member of the Presidency or somebody else from the Presidency staff but they could also come from other state institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Akmadzic, you indicated that up until one point, it was fully functioning in accordance with the rules of procedure. Did there come a time when it stopped functioning in a proper fashion and if so, to your understanding, what were the reasons?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: Apart from this aspect of the functioning of the Presidency which was fully in accordance with the law, there was another stage in the lifespan of the Presidency that we could describe as the prewar stage because at that time, the Presidency was often in session, in constant session, up until the 20th of December, 1992, and then the war broke out and the Serb members of the Presidency left the Presidency. And then on the 20th of December, 1992, the president of the Presidency, Alija Izetbegovic, did not accept the constitutional provision and the provision of the rules of procedure and refused to hand over his office to another member of the Presidency that would thus become the president and in accordance with the rotation principle, it was to be a Croat. This disrupted the work of the Presidency. Instead of the Serb members of the Presidency who had left the Presidency, now there were other representatives of the Serb people who had not, however, been elected. They had not won the election.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me stop you here and let's go through the documents and let's see if we can amplify on that. If the usher could give him the documents, the first binder would be fine and I will be referring to 1D 01408. We're going to go rather quickly with some of these documents. This is a decision -- this is in binder 1 for everybody, 1D 01408 it's 10 November 1992, we see a decision, that's to elect you as prime minister; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Go to the next document, 1D 02873, 2873. That would be in binder 3. We've seen this before, Your Honours, with the previous witness but that would be the very next document for you, sir. All your documents are in order so 1D 02873. We see here this is dated 2 August 1993, I'm fast forwarding and this is a letter which apparently you signed where you indicated that you and other members, Franjo Boras and Mr. Lasic were -- had decided not to take part in the work on the Presidency until the offensive operation of the Muslim army against the Croat population stopped. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: I remember this document. I signed it together with Mr. Franjo Boras and with Mr. Miro Lasic who were members of the Presidency and at that time, I was not a member of the Presidency. That was the 2nd of August, 1993, I was an official of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. You were the prime minister at the time, were you not?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I was the prime minister and a member of the Presidency in my capacity as the prime minister ex officio, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And that's because there was a War Presidency at the time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. At that time, and I failed to mention that in my previous answers, there was this War Presidency which increased by three more members the president of the government or the prime minister, the speaker of the assembly, and the commander of the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina which existed at that time so ex officio as the prime minister, I became a member of the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, this letter, we don't need to spend too much time on it, but were you resigning with this letter?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: No. This letter was not tantamount to resignation, but it was a warning to the Presidency that it should act in accordance with the law pass decisions in accordance with the law and that as the supreme commander of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina it should take measures to put a stop to the fighting. In this case, it was the Croat people that was being attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And then if we look at the next document, which is 1D 02673, we see that -- and this is dated -- 2673, this is in binder 3, Your Honours. This is dated 27 August 1993, and we see that the president of the Presidency, Alija Izetbegovic, is relieving you of your duties; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was relieved from my duty as the prime minister and automatically I was no longer a member of the Presidency and the explanation as given here was because of the withdrawal of the Croatian Democratic Union members from the state organs of Bosnia and Herzegovina but in accordance with the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the president can be replaced in two ways. The first way is for him to resign and the other one is for him to be held responsible for something and then the appropriate procedure must be followed and proceedings must be instituted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: To your understanding, were appropriate proceedings followed in this case?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: No. This was done in contravention of the law and the rules that applied in the Presidency and in the state as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Before we go any further, could you explain to us your relationship with Mr. Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: I welcomed Mr. Izetbegovic to the Presidency after the 1990 elections. I acquainted him with the situation in the Presidency and with the manner in which the previous Presidency functioned. Mr. Izetbegovic heard me and we had -- we were on good terms. We were friends for a good portion of the time that we spent working together. The president of the Presidency, Mr. Izetbegovic, after the war broke out, embarked on something that we could call a parallel policy. He would sometimes make decisions with the core of his associates who were not actually members of the Presidency. I disagreed with this practice and so did many others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. If we could look at now document 2D 00191, 2D 00191. This would be in binder 4, Your Honours. Again, I apologise for not putting them in the order for everyone but ... This is the very next document for you, sir, the very next document. Just --

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: Mm-hm. Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You can't go wrong. Now, this is from the Balkan Odyssey by David Owen, and I'm going to read an excerpt from it from page 52 and I want you to comment on it. It's towards the middle of the page, Your Honours, and it says, and this is what Lord Owen writes: "When the Croat Mile Akmadzic was appointed as prime minister of Bosnia and Herzegovina, he made a real effort to revive the collective leadership of the Presidency. He went back to live in Sarajevo and used his previous experience as pre-war secretary to the Presidency to try to restore the authority of the Muslim-Croat coalition that had won the referendum on independence which the Serbs boycotted. But by the end of 1992, it was becoming clear to all that he would fail and that power had gone to a small group of Muslim ministers appointed by President Izetbegovic and their nominee as vice-president, Ejup Ganic. The collective Presidency as a democratic body with meaningful representation from the three constituent nations was by the autumn of 1993 no longer a reality. The real decisions were made elsewhere. We were in effect dealing with a Muslim government for a predominantly Muslim population." That's what Lord Owen wrote in his book concerning his experience in dealing with the negotiations at the time. Would you agree with Lord Owen?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, just for the record I want to make an objection to this form of questioning. This is nothing more than a leading questioning disguised as reading the statement of someone who's not in the courtroom. This exact same evidence could have been elicited from the witness by non-leading questions: What were you doing at the time? How did you find the functioning of the president? What were you doing? Did you try to -- in a non-leading way, what you were you doing to revive the work of the president, et cetera, et cetera. All of this could have been properly elicited by non-leading questions which is the proper method of proceeding on direct examination. Putting this text to him and asking him whether he agrees with it is nothing more than a rather somewhat clever way of asking a leading question. And the Prosecution objects to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Two points. One this is the exact technique that Mr. Stringer uses. In fact, I was rather amazed that he was able to get away with it so I'm trying it; and I kind of like it. Secondly, I did ask the predicate, if you go back to my previous question, you had the witness, Mr. Akmadzic, recount how there was a parallel or two-track approach, and he talked about Izetbegovic making decisions with his close associates some of whom were not there. So in the sense, the gentleman has already provided from his own experience the answer. Now we have Lord Owen validating it. I see nothing wrong with that, and I don't think that I should be prevented from even asking further questions concerning what Lord Owen has written about. So that would be my response to the Prosecution on that one, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a moment, please. You both are right. But if you want to be efficient, what happens? In answer to a non-leading question, the witness said that he had been removed from his position as prime minister. He explained the reasons why that happened. Lord Owen wrote a book and confirms what has been said. Mr. Karnavas could have said, well, let me submit this document to you towards the middle of the page, there is a passage, could you read it and tell me whether it corresponds or not to what you said earlier and he would have said that's exactly what I said. So objections based on common law principles, why not but if you want to be efficient, it is better to go to the bottom of the matter. Mr. Stringer is not here today. He used the same technique once. Very well. Mr. Scott, you may say whatever you want but Lord Owen's book seems to confirm what the witness said. If you want the Defence to spend hours asking the witness whether he heard about Lord Owen, he would have said yes. Do you know whether he wrote a book or not? The result would be the same anyway. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just to clarify, to the extent that Mr. -- I wasn't necessarily in the courtroom and haven't been in the courtroom of course at all times when Mr. Stringer has examined witnesses but my understanding is that the -- any reference to Mr. Stringer using such a method that was done during cross-examination and leading questions or proper on what is bona fide as opposed to artificial cross-examination, number one. It's a dramatically different rule in procedure and practice as Mr. Karnavas knows under the common law system. Secondly, Your Honour, with great respect to the time pressures of this institution, not everything can be governed by efficiency. We would have no other rules. There are rules that have to be followed, yes, it would be proper -- it would be more efficient to put leading questions to every witness; as a matter of fact, it would be more efficient to do away with the witnesses and just let the lawyers talk, but that's not our system. There are rules to be followed and we cannot constantly appeal what's more efficient. Because if it's more efficient, let's do away with everything, we don't need witnesses, we'll bring books, we'll take turns reading from Lord Owen's book and we'll read that and we don't need -- that's the most efficient of all so with great respect to Mr. Karnavas, and to the Chamber, a constant appeals to efficiency do not answer the questions of principle and the rule of law in this institution or elsewhere and my objection stands, and we could have proceeded a way that this could have been elicited by non-leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours, the Petkovic Defence would wish to support Mr. Karnavas on this matter and we clearly have, although this is clearly Mr. Karnavas's witness, we clearly have a direct vested interest because such ground rules and practices are going to be established in the course of Mr. Karnavas's case are likely to apply by the same token throughout the Defence case. What we note is that although Mr. Karnavas picked Mr. Stringer's examination as the example today and studiously avoided any issue between himself and Mr. Scott which we welcome and applaud, in fact, the technique was adopted consistently throughout the Prosecution case because I recall, and I wasn't even here at the very beginning of the trial; but I recall numerous occasions particularly when a United Nations document and other documents of that nature were put to witnesses and the witness was asked after having quite a long passage put to him, is that consistent with your recollection? Fundamentally that is absolutely no different at all whether it's a passage from a book and so on and there was some objection at times we did think it was carried to extremes but that technique was adopted consistently throughout and what sauce for the goose is sauce or all the ganders on this side of the court, Your Honours, and Mr. Karnavas should be allowed to put questions in precisely that form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to ask my colleagues what they think of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber has deliberated and states that at this stage of the examination in chief, the counsel, based on documents or books is allowed to show references to a witness by referring to the document and ask questions based on that. Of course as to the probative value, the Trial Chamber will assess it in the light of the types of questions raised. Mr. Karnavas, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we go on to the next document -- I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Akmadzic, you didn't answer. You owe us an answer, a complete one.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: First of all, affirmative. What Lord Owen said, this was true although this was a compliment that he paid me, I would like to provide another explanation. Lord Owen got this impression based on the negotiations that we had at the international peace conference of the former Yugoslavia, but he was not a member of the Presidency and he doesn't quite know what went on inside the Presidency but it's precisely what Lord Owen said. Mr. Izetbegovic specifically at this time in 1993 once his term had expired and he stopped being president of the Presidency in a legal sense, also under the rules of procedure, he in some way assumed the function of head of state. He took decisions independently or within a very small circle of people. He acted very much like this at the international level and during international negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we go on to the next document, and it's 1D 00942. This would be in binder 1, Your Honours. You will see that this is a platform for the activities of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina and this, if we look at page 2, it says, it's 26 June 1992. Do you recognise this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, this says this is the document -- this is the platform for the activities. And for those of us who don't understand or don't know what a platform is, can you please tell us, what was this supposed to be?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: This document was supposed to show and to specify how negotiations should be held internationally, how Bosnia and Herzegovina's interests should be promoted. And also, how the Presidency should be informed about this and how decisions should be taken of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina as an institution and so is the country itself. It represents all of its peoples, three constituent ones, specifically. One of the representatives represented the remaining population that didn't fall under the one those three ethnic groups. We called them minorities, ethnic minorities or maybe those who refused to declare their nationality. All those who went to negotiate on behalf of the Presidency had to operate in keeping with the constitution and the Presidency's platform.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if we look at under number one: What kind of Bosnia and Herzegovina? And if we look at the second part of this paragraph, I'll read it, it says: "The internal structure of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as a multi-national and multi-religious community, is based on regional and local self-rule which recognises economic, cultural, historical, and ethnic criteria. Local and regional self-rule cannot be in opposition to the principles of territorial integrity and the unform functioning of government in the whole of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina." My question to you, sir, is: To your understanding what is this platform, this part of the platform, what is it talking about? How can we interpret this or understand this, I should say?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: There are two ways of looking at this, if you ask me. The first is the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina as the head of state is operating as a collective head of state and performs the function of the head of state and it also applies to other central bodies of the state. However, there is one thing that we mustn't forget, that is the interests declared here in terms of local self-government and government specifically in other parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's go on to the next document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a follow-up question so that we don't have to go back to this document later on. Witness, I was going to call you Mr. Prime Minister on account of your previous position. It appears from the platform that there's a very clear reference to local institutions, to local and regional self-rule. From what I can read, it seems that local and regional self-rule would be competent for economic, cultural, and ethnical criteria. This is a document that was created on the 26th of June, 1992 at the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina. When reading it, as far as you can see, don't you think that it shows that some kind of regional self-rule is acknowledged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bosnia and Herzegovina, at various stages of its existence, had different kinds of local self-government. The smallest unit was the local commune. A rung up the latter from that was the municipality. Municipalities could join forces in order to form associations of municipalities. This was based on a number of criteria and some of them are noted here. However, what we did not find noted here were communication criteria, geographic criteria and other criteria as well. Municipalities grouped together like that would normally be called an association municipalities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You seem to say that in history, there had been associations of municipalities already. Do you have a specific historic reference to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about back in the socialist times and then after then; however, back in socialism, these were called districts, counties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question: When municipalities met in Grude, it may be that the defence teams will go back to this question, but when they met in Grude, in order to create the Croatian Council which is later to become the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, is this the framework in which municipalities were going to gather and create a structure of the type that we have with the Croatian community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think so. I'm not 100 per cent certain, but I think what you're asking me about, Mr. President, is in reference to the war, the community that was established during the war. This decision invokes the provisions specified here. Nonetheless, its primary purpose, if my understanding is correct, was not just linking up but also creating the right conditions to defend Bosnia and Herzegovina, its sovereignty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. Please proceed, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if we go to the next document, P 00743, that's in binder 4, Your Honour, P 00743, that's the next document, we see this is dated 14 December 1992, these are minutes from the HDZ 2nd General Convention and you already told us that it was at 14 December when you were elected one of the vice-presidents and we can see that in this document. If you look on page 6, Your Honours, the pages are on the bottom right-hand corner we see your name. More importantly, I just wish to point out to the Court's attention, perhaps you can comment that at this particular gathering, you spoke and at least we have some minutes, this would be on page 5, Your Honours, under number 13, we see your name, Mile Akmadzic, BiH prime minister is proud to be is part of the Croatian nation, it says "naciona," and then it says, "He asks for support to BiH government from HDZ." Sir, did they accurately recount what you had indicated that you were asking HDZ to support the BiH government? And this is back in 14 December 1992? Was that your attitude at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: At the time or just before I had been appointed prime minister, I sought the support of the Croatian democratic community of Bosnia and Herzegovina for the government for the Presidency for the functioning of the state institutions in Bosnia and Herzegovina but the HDZ was one of the three winning parties in the elections along with the SDA and the SDS. As a member that party, as a member of that ethnic group, I meant to seek their support for the functioning of a government that I then left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we go to the next document and that's 1D 02892 that's the very next document in the binder that's in binder 3, Your Honours. 1D 02892, if you could look at it, sir, it's dated 28 January 1993. If we look at the second page, we see your name as the president of the government, Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I wish to direct everyone's attention to the very last paragraph of this document on page 1 and you state here, this is an address that you made to the Organisation of the Islamic Conference, this is a letter. Now, do you recall sending this letter, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, in this letter, you say at the last paragraph on the first page, "On the other hand, the representatives of the Muslim people in BH do not yet have a understandable policy and insist on a unitary Bosnia and Herzegovina that is impossible." What do you mean by that, "a unitary Bosnia and Herzegovina"?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: When I was appointed prime minister, the government platform said that Bosnia and Herzegovina had to be decentralised state, only as such could it go on existing, only as such could Bosnia and Herzegovina be possible. Any other kind of Bosnia and Herzegovina would have to be based on a unitary organisation if its constituent peoples did not get the respect they deserved, the country itself would have been impossible to preserve. Something had to be done to keep this from happening. I sent this letter to the Islamic conference, the secretary general in person. I knew that Mr. Izetbegovic enjoyed a great deal of respect in those circles, and that was why I sought their support.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But when you say unitary organisation, just so we understand, if you could just answer my question: What did you mean by that? What's a "unitary organisation"?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: Unitary means without extensive local self-government, without state-run principles that we talked about then within the Vance-Owen Plan and other plans on how Bosnia and Herzegovina should be organised. I'm talking about a regional approach where there would be regions, provinces or whatever we choose to call them and those would be established and based on all the criteria that were being negotiated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And in fact, if we go to page 2, in the middle of the third line you say, "The Croatian people seek an independent BH consisting of a number of provinces with a high degree democracy, equality for all three peoples ..." that's what you're just telling us; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. Absolutely. This is the position that we advocated and this never changed throughout the war or throughout all the rounds of international negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And we see later on in the third paragraph in the middle of it, you say: "In the same sense, we ask you to positively influence the Muslim leadership in BH to cooperate closer with the leadership of the Croatian people in BH and with the Republic of Croatia which is our common dear ally and is threatened by the same aggressor."

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, this was a time of war. We Croats did not walk out in the Presidency, two Serb members of the Presidency as I said who had been legally appointed did walk out. The Croat members of the Presidency and me as the prime minister and a member of the War Presidency remained in our positions. We were adamant that there should be international recognition for Bosnia and Herzegovina, a country that would reflect interests of all of its three peoples not just the Muslim and the Serb peoples but the Croat peoples but also the Serbs regardless of the fact that this was an act of aggression. We asked the Islamic conference the following intervention by Mr. Izetbegovic to accept these negotiations and to accept any agreement reached.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, this Islamic conference, did it send you a reply to that letter of January 1993? Did you receive an answer or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never got a response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Another question, Witness. We have seen the platform of the War Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina a short while ago, and I wonder whether you could elaborate a bit on the relationship between what you say here about the Muslim intentions and what is said in the war platform which clearly does refer to self-government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Self-government was defined quite vaguely in the platform. We adopted the platform, nonetheless; however, if you look at this document you have international negotiations and the situation which dictated that we be as specific as possible, we had to be specific about our desires. All of our three peoples wanted to be specific about what sort a country we wanted and though international negotiations at the time, we reached a conclusion at least we Croats did and I don't think any of the other groups were far from our conclusions that the best way to organise Bosnia and Herzegovina would be in terms of provinces or on the basis of provinces. As soon as the 4th January 1993 we had signed all the constitutional principles for organising Bosnia and Herzegovina. There were nine such principles. One of those principles were the provinces and now we were adamant, and we explicitly sought that the principles that were signed and accepted by all the three peoples, the Serbs, the Croats and the Muslims that those principles now be implemented in the way that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the last part of the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You may need to repeat the last part your answer, sir. You need to slow down a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Yes, if I may say the same request, which was the last line mentioned by Mr. Karnavas that -- that I would like to ask the witness to slow down and really to save the interpreters in a way that they should follow you and be so kind to make pauses between your answers and the -- I believe that it would be very useful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: May I continue? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, the next document I just put in here just to highlight some of the problems that might have come your way. This is 1D 02859, 1D 02859, this is a letter that is addressed to you. This is in binder 3, Your Honours. You may -- I'm told that there's a possibility that you may not have it, 2589. If that's the case, I will skip it and go on to the next. You don't have it? We do have copies, I'm told. Perhaps -- make sure that the Prosecution has one too. Okay. Do you have the document, 1D 02859, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We see that it's addressed to you, sir. If we look at the third page, we see that it's by a Dr. Josip Goluza. Did you know this gentleman?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm not getting an interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if you look at -- who was this individual?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: This individual was an assistant minister. He was in charge of economic relations. He was also in charge of the functioning of pressure groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now if we look at number 2, I'm just going to highlight a couple of points. Now as I understand, it's translated that he was in charge of the functioning of pressure groups. That's what has been translated. Is that what you meant "pressure groups" or are you speaking of logistic centres?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: Logistics centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if you just relax, sir, I will point you to the document. Just relax a little bit. If you look at paragraph 2, it says: "Humanitarian aid arriving from abroad from various donors is under no control. Logistic centres which are currently in the process of establishment, should restore order especially in the control of and distribution of humanitarian aid." If we go to paragraph 3, it says: "Donors of humanitarian aid both in the country and abroad are known in most cases, however, donations of financial assistance are unknown. The government has opened 12 accounts around Europe to which financial means should be paid. I claim with full responsibility that these funds are not on those accounts, except for $440.000 US dollars sent to the office of the government of the republic of BiH in Zagreb by selling goods ..." and it goes on. Sir, I guess my question is were you aware of these problems and why do we have these problems and perhaps you could tell us when -- when was this sent to you or to your office?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: This was actually handed over to me when I travelled to Zagreb once. I submitted this to the government because I had been involved in negotiations all the time for this to be decided. This is a result of work that was parallel with the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Logistics centres were opened, aid continued to arrive. This wasn't fully state-controlled.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm just going to stop you. Why was there such chaos when you look at this document, it's very clear that money is disappearing, goods are not being controlled. Who is at fault? Why are these problems occurring? And this is while you're the prime minister of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I wanted to give Mr. Karnavas a fair chance to ask follow-up questions so I stayed in my seat, but I would still like to get the answer to the question of approximate date or time because again the Chamber knows it makes a dramatic deference as to when we are talking about. I do note that in paragraph 3 of the letter, it makes reference to the president of the government at that time being Mr. Pelivan and I believe that Mr. Pelivan stopped being the prime minister or president of the government sometime in October 1992. If that assists the witness or the Chamber but perhaps Mr. Karnavas could ask additional questions on the time of this or date of this letter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It hadn't escaped me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You were prime minister, as you indicated, from November 10th, 1992 to approximately the end of August 1993. Do you know about when this was sent to your office?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: This letter was sent to my office early 1993. I was prime minister and there was this one report that I think is about the period of Mr. Jure Pelivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. We'll go on to the next document, 1D 02869. That's in binder 3, Your Honours. 1D 02869. That's the very next document. It's dated 17 July 1993, we're moving forward but staying with you, this is a letter or a statement and a meeting of prime ministers of the Central European Initiative in Budapest on 17 July 1993. Do you recognise this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is my document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And what was the event, very briefly?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: Bosnia and Herzegovina, as a member of the Central European Initiative, it's a group of about ten countries from central Europe and the Balkans for the most part. They were holding a meeting with prime ministers and foreign ministers involved. This was at Budapest around this time, the 17th of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if you go to page 3, we look at the first -- the paragraph in the middle of the page. Towards the latter part of that paragraph, you state: "It is possible for Bosnia and Herzegovina to be a decentralised state made up of several constituent units with a free flow of people, goods and capital over its entire territory." Was that your position then as you were stating it?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: That was precisely my position and that's the position that I presented at the Central European Initiative. I sought their support and I received their support in principle. Other prime ministers presented such views. This meeting was attended by Mr. Silajdzic too, the foreign minister. He, himself, agreed with this view.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, as I understand it, you participated in several of the peace initiatives; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Of all the peace initiatives that you were involved in and you were aware of, which of the ones -- which of all of them did you find most acceptable for Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: Since I was on good terms with Mr. Izetbegovic, regardless of the fact that I opposed his term of office as the president after the 20th of December, 1992, I told him and that was the position that I presented in various international forums that Bosnia and Herzegovina is a state of three constituent peoples with equal status, a state that is not Serbian, not Croat, not Muslim, but a state that belongs to all those ethnic communities, it was a Serb, Muslim and Croat state, could continue to exist as a decentralised state and that the best kind of system for it was the system that was reached at the Geneva negotiations held under the auspices of the International Conference For the Former Yugoslavia. The co-chairmen of the steering committee were Cyrus Vance as a representative of the United Nations and Lord Owen as a representatives of the European Union or community.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. We'll take a break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll have the break now and resume at ten past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, if we could go on to the next document, 1D 02884. That would be in binder number 3, Your Honours. Do you have it, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it's dated July 20th, 1993. You can see that on the second page, there is a stamp and your name and the signature. Is that your signature, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And apparently this seems to be a letter to the editor where you are explaining that -- that you felt compelled, I guess, to explain certain issues that were being reported at the time. Do you stand behind what you indicated in this particular letter, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, on page 2, very quickly, I don't have time to go through the entire letter, but on page 2 at the second to last paragraph, penultimate, I guess if you want to use the farcy word, "Bosnian government opposes sanctions against Croatia, sanctions on Croatia would be a deathnell for Bosnia." Now, you say Bosnian government opposes sanctions against Croatia." Can you explain that, sir, because at the time, you were the prime minister as I understand it?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was the prime minister. Sanctions would not have been good for Bosnia and Herzegovina since Bosnia and Herzegovina shares about two-fourths of its borders with Croatia and regardless of their conflicts, its political and economic and human ties with Croatia were very strong. To impose sanctions on Croatia would in fact reflect on Bosnia and Herzegovina too. It would have repercussions, it would be tantamount to imposing sanctions on Bosnia and Herzegovina and that was not in its interest, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, just let me touch on another issue. We've heard testimony here and we've seen documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have the document here on the screen. On page 2, first paragraph, this is what you seem to say, sir, you claim that the incidents or the clashes that oppose the two armies seem to be the result of the international community's implicit support for Serb genocide against Bosnian Muslims. Could you tell us what you meant by that? By reading that sentence, I'm under the impression that the state of war in your country would be due to the Serbs who were committing a genocide against the Muslims. Am I right in saying that or is your interpretation different from what I just said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At any rate, the war in my country was the result of an aggression by Serbia and the army of Yugoslavia, Yugoslav people's army and of Montenegro on Bosnia Herzegovina. The Presidency --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you mention clashes between the two armies, do you mean the HVO and the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in this case I'm talking about the HVO and the BH army but this conflict was the result of the aggression that I mentioned and even before this conflict, the thing that we discussed at the Presidency and the government actually came about, the aggression in particular in eastern Bosnia where there was no HVO for all intents and purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Karnavas, I would like to have a follow-up question. The witness just mentioned that -- and I quote from the very last paragraph there: "We discussed at the Presidency and the government and actually came about that the aggression in particular in eastern Bosnia where there was no HVO ..." et cetera. Now my question is the following very briefly, that this July 20th letter which you sent to the New York Times, was it in a way agreed upon by the War Presidency and did you discuss this kind of statements of political nature, of course, very important to us with the Presidency or with President Izetbegovic? So it is my question if you have held a position formulated in a way jointly with the War Presidency. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina in its full composition defined the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The war was defined as follows: The war in Bosnia and Herzegovina is the result of an aggression on the part of what was Serbian Montenegro at that time or rather that was the federal republic of Yugoslavia, the Yugoslav People's Army which still existed or rather at the beginning it still existed at this time it did not exist anymore and the internal paramilitary forces organized by the Serbian Democratic Party and by the Serb people in Bosnia and Herzegovina. This aggression was aimed at Bosnia and Herzegovina and there were cases of genocide in eastern Bosnia, that's what we were saying at the time and there was aggression throughout the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This aggression indirectly led to the conflict between the Croatian Defence Council and the BH army because the areas that Croats and Muslims were left with were reduced, in particular, in Central Bosnia and in Herzegovina where the Muslim people started to move from Jajce towards Central Bosnia and towards southern Herzegovina, the Neretva River area. Given this imbalance in the ethnic composition, the shifts in the ethnic composition first we saw those sporadic clashes which then escalated into large-scale conflict but we never used the term "war" to describe them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I have two technical questions. The first one refers to the fact that this is a government document where normally one takes all the pains to write them properly. And it appears to me that the date on top of the letter has been amended, that it was typed "1992" and someone then by hand changed the 2 to a 3. Now, can you comment on this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was just a typo. I made this correction by hand because on the 20th of July, 1992 I was not the prime minister at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You were not the prime minister but you signed as -- or you used at least the letterhead -- the letterhead of the prime minister and made the letter appear as the letter of the prime minister?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, he indicated that he corrected it to 1993 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Because on July 20, 1992 he was not -- yes. That is -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you look at the second page, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then there is a letter attached to it that says July 20, 1993 by Mr. V. Miles Ragus as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I just wanted to make it clear. The second question is was this letter printed? Did it appear in the New York Times?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, we didn't receive New York Times on a regular basis, so I can't really tell you that. I hope it was published but I cannot confirm that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And later on, you never tried to find out? I mean you must have had personnel and there are search machines, at least later on. I can imagine that you had other business to worry about. I'm just curious.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, in late August 1993, I was removed from office. The Muslim element in the Bosnian authorities took over control of everything. I found it difficult to obtain my own personnel file.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we're still talking about this document, on the 23rd of July, the diplomat who is a member of your permanent mission in New York addresses your letter to the New York Times. Since your letter was not directly sent to the New York Times, it first went via your embassy. If it went via your embassy, your embassy mentions that you're one of the Croatian members of the Presidency which means that it is your country that is involved, not only you as a Croat because the representation of your country officially sends this letter to the New York Times. Am I right in saying that? Am I right in drawing that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are indeed right, Your Honour. The permanent mission of Bosnia and Herzegovina in New York had its permanent representative or ambassador who was a Muslim, Mr. Sacirbey. There was some other personnel too, people who worked in the embassy including Mr. Miles Raguz. He was an American born in Bosnia and Herzegovina and he escorted me at all times while I was in New York. And I asked him to forward this letter on my behalf and that's what he did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. Perhaps we'll get back to some of the content on that letter later on but let's move on to the next document, 1D 02906, 2906, this is the very next document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, I was again waiting to see if there would be further questions on the document. Before we pass on to the next document, I only observe for Judge Prandler's benefit and Judge Prandler can decide, of course, for himself whether he wants to persist in his question but there was no answer to the question about whether the letter was produced jointly with other members of the Presidency. I can certainly come back to it in cross-examination but Judge Prandler, I don't believe you received an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Actually, I confirmed the situation but since my question was followed by my fellow Judge's questions, I didn't wish to have something, a kind of follow-up on my question itself, but that is indeed an important issue if the War Presidency knew about the letter itself and it is not only about this letter frankly, but my question is in general, if there was a kind of day-to-day coordination and cooperation between the War Presidency and of course the prime minister's office, that is the witness's office involved on those questions of importance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately not. There was no daily coordination. It was very difficult to live in Sarajevo. That was the first problem. There was another problem. I, and some other Presidency members, were constantly involved in peace talks about Bosnia and Herzegovina. We travelled to Zagreb, to Geneva, to Brussels, to New York, to Washington, and to all other major centres where various talks were being held. So it was impossible to have this kind of communication. That is why we, the Croats, proposed that the Presidency, in accordance with the regulation in force in Bosnia and Herzegovina should leave Sarajevo and move to a place where it could work despite the war and there was a proposal for it to move to Livno because there were secure premises there that existed from the time of the Yugoslav People's Army. Mr. Izetbegovic rejected this proposal and he rejected the proposal to have a corridor linking Sarajevo with the rest of the world or the rest of the state although Sarajevo was completely besieged, it was under siege. We travelled to the airport in armoured personnel carriers, UN vehicles, and then we would leave on humanitarian relief flights. My deputy, Hakija Turajlic a Muslim, was killed en route from the airport to Sarajevo having seen off the foreign minister, the Turkish foreign minister. He was killed in the armoured vehicle. Your Honours, for the better part of the war, we in Sarajevo did not have any electricity. We didn't have water. We didn't have any food or heating. We couldn't leave our homes. And in general, the living conditions were harsh. People would bury their children in front of their own houses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you. Continue, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
